issues.legal_issue: An appellate court hearing an accused’s appeal against conviction cannot overturn an unappealed acquittal on a separate charge and convict the accused of an offence arising from that charge.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused of the direct murder charge but convicted him of murder on a constructive-liability basis.
The State did not appeal the acquittal on the direct murder charge.

In the accused’s appeal against his convictions, the High Court set aside the constructive-liability conviction but substituted a conviction for a lesser direct offence and maintained the life sentence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court acted without jurisdiction when it convicted the accused of a direct offence despite the unappealed acquittal on the direct charge; that conviction and sentence had to be set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 423(1)(a) and 423(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, an appeal against conviction concerns the conviction under challenge and does not empower the appellate court to reverse an acquittal on another charge. Reversal of an acquittal requires the procedure prescribed for that purpose, including under section 439. The Court applied State of Andhra Pradesh v. Thadi Narayana.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and trial_acquittal_on_direct_offense and state_did_not_appeal_acquittal and appellate_court_substituted_direct_offense

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The accused brought an appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.trial_acquittal_on_direct_offense: The trial court acquitted the accused of the direct offence.
predicates.state_did_not_appeal_acquittal: The prosecution did not appeal the acquittal on the direct offence.
predicates.appellate_court_substituted_direct_offen: The appellate court replaced or supplemented the challenged conviction with a conviction for a direct offence covered by the acquittal.

issues.definition: When an accused appeals a conviction, the appellate court cannot convict the accused on a direct offence covered by an acquittal that the prosecution did not appeal.

issues.legal_issue: Constructive liability based on membership in an unlawful assembly is a distinct offence from direct liability for the underlying offence.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused of the direct murder charge but convicted him of murder on the basis of membership in an unlawful assembly with the relevant common object.
The High Court treated the constructive-liability charge as permitting it to substitute a direct-offence conviction.
issues.conclusion: A charge of constructive liability is legally distinct from a charge of committing the offence directly, and a conviction on the constructive-liability charge does not authorize conviction for the direct offence.
issues.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code creates a specific and distinct offence, rather than merely enabling the imposition of vicarious liability. A charge based on section 302 read with section 149 is distinct from a charge under section 302 alone. The Court relied on Barendra Kumar Ghosh v. Emperor, Queen v. Sabid Ali, Nanak Chand v. State of Punjab, and Suraj Pal v. State of Uttar Pradesh.

predicates.criminal_proceeding: The matter is a criminal trial or appeal concerning an accused’s liability for an offence.
predicates.accused_charged_with_group_liability_for: The accused was charged with liability for an offence based on the conduct of members of a group.
predicates.charge_alleges_membership_in_unlawful_as: The charge alleges that the accused belonged to an unlawful assembly with a common object connected to the offence.

issues.definition: A charge alleging group liability based on membership in an unlawful assembly with a common object identifies an offence distinct from committing the underlying offence directly.
